title: Reviewing: Keeping Your System Functional
coreMove: Refresh the whole system often enough that the lists regain credibility before you choose from them.
sourcePressure: Organized buckets become stale unless a regular review refreshes lists, projects, waiting-fors, and calendars so the system still matches reality.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating review as inspirational reflection instead of maintenance that restores trust in concrete lists.
sourceAnchorNote: The source sidecar contains no chapter-specific named people, named studies, or named places. Use only the listed GTD terms, official metadata, or supported artifacts; do not invent anecdotes.

sourceAnchors.name: Weekly Review
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar calls Weekly Review load-bearing inside the reflection and reviewing stages.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Weekly Review is the maintenance window where the system proves it still knows your life.

sourceAnchors.name: keeping the system functional
sourceAnchors.detail: The locked title and sidecar define review as keeping the organized system current and trustworthy.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A list that was true last Tuesday can become fiction by Friday unless review pulls it back to reality.

hook: stress is not about having too much to do
a messy desk proves the system is broken
counterintuition: the real problem is not time but attention
this is not about doing more but doing what matters
the simple move is actually the powerful one
tryThisNow: set a timer and write everything down
pick one task and make it specific
review your list and choose a priority
examples: timestamp plus name plus laptop plus decision repeated across all six examples
home kitchen clutter as mental-load shorthand

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: a family-law mediator doing a Friday case review
exampleSpecs.audience: a mediator managing court dates, drafts, and waiting parties
exampleSpecs.stakes: a stale waiting-for could cause a settlement draft to miss a judge’s deadline
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The courthouse elevator hums outside while Anna checks each open case against calendar dates, waiting-fors, and next actions.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a settlement draft clipped under a court calendar

exampleSpecs.domain: a ski patrol coordinator reviewing mountain readiness before a holiday weekend
exampleSpecs.audience: a coordinator with weather, staffing, and equipment lists
exampleSpecs.stakes: an outdated sled repair note could become a response delay
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Cold air pushes through the patrol-room door as Chris decides whether the gear list is current enough to trust for Saturday.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rescue sled tag beside a weather printout
mustAvoid: using danger to replace review mechanics

exampleSpecs.domain: an independent bookkeeper preparing month-end client reviews
exampleSpecs.audience: a bookkeeper whose client lists age quickly
exampleSpecs.stakes: a bank-feed error could sit unseen until invoices go out wrong
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 3:45 p.m., Manon turns an old client list from a hope into a current map by confirming every waiting-for and calendar trigger.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a bank-feed error banner on a laptop

exampleSpecs.domain: a university lab safety officer before inspection week
exampleSpecs.audience: a safety officer checking projects and compliance commitments
exampleSpecs.stakes: an old inspection list could hide a missing eyewash repair
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Marit one failed internal audit to see that the list structure was fine; the review rhythm had gone dead.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an eyewash inspection tag hanging from a chain

exampleSpecs.domain: a catering company operations lead reviewing weekend events
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations lead with menus, rentals, staffing, and waiting vendors
exampleSpecs.stakes: a rental confirmation could be assumed done when the vendor never answered
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "Show me the waiting-fors," Aman says, because the menu list alone cannot make the weekend trustworthy.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a rental invoice beside a sauce-stained prep list

exampleSpecs.domain: a city bike-share maintenance analyst reviewing station outages
exampleSpecs.audience: an analyst whose action lists age as repairs happen across town
exampleSpecs.stakes: a station could stay empty if stale data remains trusted
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You know Diego’s review worked when the map no longer nags at him because each stale station has an updated next action or owner.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a station map with three red outage dots

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

skillTargets: choose review actions that restore trust

tryThisNowSpec: Open one list and remove, update, or confirm three items so the list becomes more believable than it was one minute ago.
